newsitem.title: CHINA: China yuan market volume up on debt trade control.
newsitem.headline: China yuan market volume up on debt trade control.

text.p: Daily turnover on China's local currency interbank market has risen sharply in recent weeks thanks to official measures aimed at reducing volatility in the state debt trading markets, analysts said on Tuesday.

Average daily turnover on the Shanghai-based interbank market is now around 2.9 billion yuan ($350 million), up from an average of around 2.5 billion yuan a day in its first year of operation last year.

The state banks have been told to stop trading on the secondary state debt market and are increasingly transferring funds to the interbank market, set up early last year to provide a channel for trading short-term funds.
"The recent crackdown on the state debt market has made the interbank market a more important source of short-term money supply," one interbank trader said.
The state banks were previously active players in the state debt secondary markets, particularly the state debt repurchase market which is an important source of funds for stock speculation.

Another measure that has dampened state debt secondary market activity is the establishment last month of a central state debt depository, responsible for holding, clearing and settling all state debt transactions.
The setting-up of the depository has been a blow to many institutions that had been using state debt certificates for multiple trades on different markets simultaneously.

"The set-up of the central depository has made state banks clearly realise that in the mid-term, there is no alternative but to stop trading on the state debt secondary market," said a state debt trader.
"Banks have especially been affected due to the recent crackdown and we have begun to do more business on the interbank market," said one Beijing-based banker with a major Chinese state bank.
The interbank market was launched in early 1996 to allow banks and other financial institutions to move short-term money of up to 120 days duration amongst themselves.

Early this year, major state banks were told by the People's Bank of China, the central bank, to gradually stop trading on the state debt secondary market, to effectively check bank money from flowing into the stock markets.
Official statistics show a sharp increase in daily turnover during the past two weeks with more and more bank money flowing into the market.

Another factor pushing volumes up is the recent admission of selected foreign banks into the system. China has approved nine foreign banks to do local currency business and most of them now trade on the interbank market, traders said.
But despite the rising volume on the interbank market, activity is still far too small to allow the market to become a real barometer of China's short-term money movements, analysts said.

A key problem is restricted membership. Beijing has allowed only a limited number of banks and short-term financial centres, money brokerages run by the central bank, to be full members allowed to trade directly on the market.
Other players, the second-tier members of the market, can only trade through the short-term financing centres.
The central government has promised a dramatic expansion of the interbank market this year including more first-tier members.
